title: Landing Pattern and Trim Awareness
summary: Normal takeoff review, local departures, trim malfunctions, and landing pattern fundamentals.
overview: This event builds on the first contact sim by adding trim-malfunction awareness and a full landing-pattern framework. You will continue practicing takeoff and departure procedures while learning how to recognize inadvertent trim inputs, manage pattern geometry, and fly no-flap, takeoff-flap, and landing-flap patterns with the right power and airspeed picture.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items
studyNotes.summary: The big themes are recognizing bad trim early, keeping the pattern standardized, and making configuration changes at the right time instead of chasing the airplane late.

items.text: Normal takeoff expectations remain the same as FAM3101: disciplined lineup flow, correct rotation at 90 KIAS, and timely gear and flap retraction.
Area departure procedures still require early compliance with runway-specific routing, local altitude restrictions, and correct radio changes.
This event assumes you can carry the takeoff and departure workflow forward while adding pattern work on top of it.
Inadvertent trim inputs are common because the HOTAS layout keeps your hands on the stick and PCL throughout dynamic phases of flight.
Possible effects include:

children.text: Unexpected nose-down trim during pull-up or rotation.
Unexpected nose-up trim during descent or pattern work.
Rudder-trim imbalance that increases drag and workload.

items.text: Recovery priorities are:

children.text: Adjust airspeed to reduce control forces.
Execute the Runaway Trim checklist if abnormal forces persist.

items.text: The goal is to stop the bad trim before it creates an unsafe pitch picture or destabilizes the pattern.
The landing pattern is a systematic sequence built around break, downwind, abeam, 180, 90, final, and landing.
Key geometry and flow points include:

children.text: Enter the overhead at 1000 feet MSL and 200 KIAS, offset to the pattern side.
Get below 150 KIAS before lowering gear.
Stabilize downwind at pattern altitude, 3/4 to 1 wingtip distance, and the correct configuration airspeed.
Transition no sooner than abeam the intended point of landing.

items.text: Pattern success depends on managing power, pitch, roll, and timely calls instead of making large corrections late.
Takeoff-flap, landing-flap, and no-flap patterns all use the same geometry, but their power settings and airspeeds differ.
No-flap patterns require the most planning because the transition is delayed and the aircraft carries more energy.
Landing-flap patterns provide the most drag and lowest final approach speed, while takeoff-flap patterns sit between landing-flap and no-flap handling.
The key is to make deliberate configuration changes and trim early rather than trying to salvage the pattern with large bank or power corrections.
